extracted.intended_audience: writers, artists, critics, and students of aesthetics or creative writing interested in producing sublime and beautiful effects
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing literary/visual effects of the sublime and the beautiful, describing sensory techniques (sound, smell, color, proportion, pain, novelty) and what does or does not produce aesthetic greatness. Useful for creative writers, rhetoricians, and artists seeking principled rules for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bright/cheerful ornament when seeking the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of gilding, mosaics, painting, or statues, contribute but little to the sublime; with a strict caution however against anything light and riant; as nothing so effectually deadens the whole taste of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for a sustained sublime effect, prefer melancholy, sombre treatments (avoid gay, ornate, or light ornamentation). Ornamental splendour can undermine the 'melancholy kind of greatness' required for the highest sublime unless uniform striking sublimity is intended in every particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and loudness as a source of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive loudness alone is sufficient to overpower the soul, to suspend its action, and to fill it with terror. The noise of vast cataracts, raging storms, thunder, or artillery, awakes a great and awful sensation in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overwhelming, vast, or overpowering sounds (natural or man-made) to induce awe or terror. The sheer force/scale of sound can create sublime emotion even without technical musical niceties; crowds' shouting or artillery likewise work by sheer sonic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness (beginning or cessation) to rouse attention
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden beginning, or sudden cessation of sound of any considerable force, has the same power. The attention is roused by this; and the faculties driven forward, as it were, on their guard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ abrupt onsets or stops, contrast, and sudden transitions in sound or sight to startle, awaken attention, and create a sense of danger or grandeur. Repetition of a single strong sound after intervals (e.g., clock striking at night, drum stroke, distant cannon) yields especially grand and awful effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermitting (low, tremulous) sounds produce terror
rubrics_metrics.description: A low, tremulous, intermitting sound ... is productive of the sublime. Some low, confused, uncertain sounds, leave us in the same fearful anxiety concerning their causes, that no light, or an uncertain light, does concerning the objects that surround us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce intermittent, low, uncertain noises (tremulous, off-and-on sounds) to exploit uncertainty and generate anxiety or sublime dread—especially effective in conjunction with darkness or partial light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative cries of animals and inarticulate human voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Such sounds as imitate the natural inarticulate voices of men, or any animals in pain or danger, are capable of conveying great ideas; ... The angry tones of wild beasts are equally capable of causing a great and awful sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cries and inarticulate vocalizations (human or animal) or sounds that imitate them to convey raw, immediate ideas of danger, pain, or majesty. These sounds often communicate universally where language cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smell and taste: bitters and intolerable stenches as sublime sources
rubrics_metrics.description: No smells or tastes can produce a grand sensation, except excessive bitters, and intolerable stenches. ... when they are moderated, as in a description or narrative, they become sources of the sublime, as genuine as any other, and upon the very same principle of a moderated pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke extreme tastes or odors (bitterness, stench) in description—carefully moderated—to contribute to sublime effect. Test whether bitter/stench images, when united with grand images, maintain dignity (they should not degrade the composition). Avoid pairing such disagreeable qualities with mean or contemptible ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling/pain as a central means to the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of bodily pain, in all the modes and degrees of labor, pain, anguish, torment, is productive of the sublime; ... that the sublime is an idea belonging to self-preservation; that it is, therefore, one of the most affecting we have; that its strongest emotion is an emotion of distress; and that no pleasure from a positive cause belongs to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke the sublime, depict or suggest bodily anguish, danger, or distress—emphasize the self-preserving instincts and associated terror rather than positive pleasure. The sublime's affective core is distress and the confrontation with peril or overwhelming forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate sound-effects from linguistic meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not mean words, because words do not affect simply by their sounds, but by means altogether different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing sonic effects for the sublime, distinguish the raw acoustic power of sounds (loudness, suddenness, intermittence) from the semantic or rhetorical power of words. Sonic properties can independently induce sublime responses without lexical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty defined as qualities that cause love (distinct from desire)
rubrics_metrics.description: By beauty, I mean that quality, or those qualities in bodies, by which they cause love, or some passion similar to it. ... I likewise distinguish love ... from desire or lust; which is an energy of the mind ... that hurries us on to the possession of certain objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for qualities that elicit 'love'—a contemplative satisfaction—rather than desire or lust. In descriptive work, preserve the sensory qualities that prompt affectionate admiration (colour, form, manner) without conflating them with appetitive impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion is not the primary cause of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty hath usually been said to consist in certain proportions of parts. ... I have great reason to doubt, whether beauty be at all an idea belonging to proportion. ... it is not measure, but manner, that creates all the beauty which belongs to shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on fixed numerical proportions (ratios, canonical measurements) as a formula for beauty. Examples across flowers, animals, and human figures show beauty arises despite widely varying measures. Focus on manner, arrangement, and expressive qualities rather than mechanical proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion fails as a universal rule across vegetables, animals, humans
rubrics_metrics.description: The rose is a large flower, yet it grows upon a small shrub; the flower of the apple is very small, and grows upon a large tree; yet the rose and the apple blossom are both beautiful ... The swan ... has a neck longer than the rest of his body ... the peacock ... has comparatively but a short neck, with a tail longer than the neck and the rest of the body taken together ... No species is so strictly confined to any certain proportions, that there is not a considerable variation amongst the individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating depictions of natural beauty, allow for wide variation; do not enforce a single proportional template. Use concrete examples (flowers, birds, humans) to justify that beauty tolerates divergent proportions—practical implication: artistic freedom in shape and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformity is opposed to common form, not to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Deformity is opposed not to beauty, but to the complete common form ... If one of the legs of a man be found shorter than the other, the man is deformed; because there is something wanting to complete the whole idea we form of a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ugliness/deformity (departure from a recognized complete form) from absence of beauty. Removing deforming defects does not automatically produce beauty; beauty is a positive quality not merely the lack of deformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom and habitual fitness do not create beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful strikes us as much by its novelty as the deformed itself. ... The effect of constant use is to make all things of whatever kind entirely unaffecting. ... the idea of fitness (utility) is not the cause of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that habitual exposure or practical utility will make something beautiful. Novelty often contributes to perceived beauty; conversely, mere usefulness or familiar proportions tend to dull the emotional effect. For writers: refresh perceptions rather than rely on conventional functional forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness (utility) is not equivalent to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: It is said that the idea of utility, or of a part's being well adapted to answer its end, is the cause of beauty ... the wedge-like snout of a swine ... the great bag hanging to the bill of a pelican ... the porcupine with his missile quills ... how well fitted is the wolf for running and leaping! how admirably is the lion armed for battle! but will any one therefore call the elephant, the wolf, and the lion, beautiful animals?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate well-adapted or useful forms with beauty. Practical adaptation (fitness) may be admirable but does not guarantee aesthetic loveliness. In depiction, emphasize expressive, affective qualities separately from mere functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test images by their dignity in association
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one of the tests by which the sublimity of an image is to be tried, not whether it becomes mean when associated with mean ideas; but whether, when united with images of an allowed grandeur, the whole composition is supported with dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining discordant or unpleasant elements (bitterness, stench, deformity) with grand imagery, judge their sublimity by whether the combined composition preserves dignity and grandeur. If the unpleasant element drags the composition into burlesque or meanness, it undermines the sublime.
